vignette: Nguyen is a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has been living with the lasting effects of torture he endured several years ago. As an accountant working in downtown Los Angeles, his days are filled with numbers and meetings that have become increasingly difficult to navigate due to his PTSD symptoms. The traumatic event itself occurred during a visit to his home country when he was detained by authorities under false pretenses and subjected to intense psychological and physical torture over several weeks. The experience has left him with profound emotional scars, particularly in the form of intrusive memories that come to mind suddenly and unbidden. These memories are like a film that replays continuously in his mind, each scene fragmented and out of sequence, leaving him feeling disoriented. One day, while attending a business meeting filled with strangers from various departments, Nguyen found himself abruptly transported back to his traumatic experience. The sound of unfamiliar voices triggered a memory that felt alien to him-like it belonged to someone else rather than to himself. This sudden intrusion was overwhelming and left him feeling profoundly unsettled. His fear of harm grew in response; he began to believe that you can never truly know who might turn out to be your next tormentor. He became hyper-vigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. The intrusive memories also intensified his belief that he had been permanently changed for the worse. Every time he tried to discuss the future with colleagues or friends, these memories would resurface, leaving him feeling both disconnected and despairing about what might lie ahead. He often wondered how someone else in a similar situation could have stopped the event from happening, further fueling his sense of helplessness. Nguyen's perception that others would cope better made him feel even more isolated. This belief contributed to his memories becoming even more vivid and confusing. The sequence of events felt jumbled, like pieces of a puzzle that he could never fully put together. This confusion reinforced his negative appraisals, creating a cycle where the intrusive memories were intensified by his fears. In his daily life as an accountant, these symptoms began to take their toll on both his personal and professional relationships. He found it increasingly difficult to engage with colleagues or clients, often avoiding conversations that could lead to discussions about future plans or interactions with strangers. His work performance suffered as he struggled to concentrate and meet deadlines, leading to strained relations with supervisors. What finally brought Nguyen to seek help was a particularly distressing incident at work where an unexpected question from a colleague triggered another intrusive memory, leaving him in a state of panic. He realized that these memories were not just disrupting his professional life but also affecting his ability to function normally. The fear that he might never feel safe again and the belief that he had been permanently damaged weighed heavily on him. Nguyen hopes that with therapy, he can find a way to cope with his intrusive memories and regain a sense of control over his life. He is determined to break free from the cycle of negative appraisals and re-engage meaningfully with his work and social environment without being constantly haunted by his past experiences.
